title: Primes up to N
directAnswer: Either trial-divide each i (O(n√n)) or run the Sieve of Eratosthenes (O(n log log n)) for larger n. Collect every i that stays prime.

remember.takeaway: Need all primes up to n? Sieve, don't trial-divide each.
remember.formula: sieve: for p where !composite[p]: cross out p*p, p*p+p, ...
whenToUse: All primes up to a bound
antiSignals: Just one primality check — use √n trial division

problemStatement: Given `n`, return all prime numbers from 2 to `n` (inclusive) as a list.
understanding: Test each candidate with trial division to √candidate, or use the Sieve of Eratosthenes for many queries.

approaches.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
List all primes from 2 to n. The efficient method is the **Sieve of Eratosthenes**: mark the multiples of each prime as composite; whatever stays unmarked is prime.

**Why the sieve beats per-number testing.** Trial-dividing every number is O(n√n). The sieve instead does the work once per prime, crossing out its multiples, giving O(n log log n) — near-linear. It's the right tool when you need *all* primes up to a bound.

**Why start crossing out at p·p.** Any multiple of p smaller than p² (like 2p, 3p, …) has a smaller prime factor and was already crossed out when that smaller prime was processed. Starting at p² avoids redundant work.

**Edge: n < 2.** No primes exist, so return an empty list. The sieve needs a boolean array of size n+1, hence O(n) space.
hints: Testing each number is O(n√n) — can you do all of them together?
Mark multiples of each found prime; unmarked numbers are prime.
Why can you start crossing out at p² instead of 2p?
approaches.insight: Naming the sieve and its near-linear complexity is the strong answer; per-number trial division is the baseline.
approaches.complexityReasoning: each prime p crosses out n/p numbers; summed over primes it's O(n log log n), with an O(n) boolean array.

java.explanation: An unmarked number is prime; record it.

java.line: for (m = p*p; m <= n; m += p)
java.explanation: Cross out its multiples, starting at p².

pitfalls: Starting the inner crossing-out at 2p instead of p² (slower but still correct).

commonMistakes: Starting the inner crossing-out at 2p instead of p² (slower but still correct).
patternNote: A core fresher pattern: Sieve of Eratosthenes. Master it on small inputs and it transfers to harder problems.
